summary: Reddit, X and Bluesky were blocked today, so this report rests on Hacker News threads only. Strongest themes: services rejecting VoIP numbers and forcing SMS 2FA, forgotten third-party scripts after the Optimizely compromise, and people who would pay for DRM-free media or just want to plug in a keyboard and play piano.

ideas.title: Will This Site Take My Number?
ideas.oneLiner: A crowd-sourced checker and extension that tells you, before you type, whether a site's signup or 2FA will reject your VoIP or Google Voice number, and what to do instead.
ideas.problem: Banks, retailers and big platforms increasingly reject VoIP numbers as 'invalid', insist on SMS 2FA, or silently overwrite the number you gave them. People who keep a VoIP line for spam control are pushed into handing out their real cell number, and nobody publishes which services accept what.
ideas.targetUsers: Privacy-minded consumers, people with a landline or VoIP-only home number, expats and travellers without a local SIM, and anyone who uses a secondary number to dodge spam calls.
ideas.monetization: Free lookup and extension; Rs 99/month or $2/month for alerts when a service you use changes its phone policy and for private notes synced across devices.
mvp: Community database of services with accepted / rejected / flaky status per number type (mobile, VoIP, Google Voice, landline)
Browser extension that shows a badge on signup and phone-entry fields
One-tap report button: 'accepted' or 'rejected' with the date
Fallback guide per service: non-SMS 2FA options, authenticator support, support-desk workaround
Watchlist that alerts you when a service you use starts rejecting your number type

competitors.name: Google Voice
competitors.gap: Free and popular, but many services reject its numbers for verification and nothing tells you which ones before you try.

competitors.name: MySudo / Hushed / Cloaked
competitors.gap: Sell secondary numbers but do not publish a reliable per-service acceptance list, so users still discover rejections by failing.

competitors.name: Generic 'is this number VoIP' lookup sites
competitors.gap: Check the number, not the destination service, so they cannot say whether a given bank or retailer will accept it.

sources.title: Comment on 'ID.me terms required for IRS sign-in'
sources.quote: I've had a bank account for about a decade which forced me to add a phone number. A year or two ago, they insisted on "re-verifying" and then said the current number was invalid for whatever reason, which I assume means I don't have it registered as a postpaid number or have opted out of some data brokers. They still insist on sending 2fa codes to it though. I'm tired of getting stuck with paid, invasive, less convenient, less secure 2fa

sources.title: Comment on 'ID.me terms required for IRS sign-in'
sources.quote: What's frustrating is that my VoIP number gives me powerful anti-spam tools - that's why I'm reluctant to get rid of it and start giving out my actual cell#!

sources.title: Comment on 'ID.me terms required for IRS sign-in'
sources.quote: Walmart deleted the house phone number I had and told me it was invalid. In actuality it is a home VoIP number that my wife also uses for her separate account and Walmart has decided that although multiple Walmart accounts are allowed per addresses a phone number can only be associated with one of them.

sources.title: Comment on 'BugMeNot has closed'
sources.quote: Nice, now I wish there'll be a service line that for phone/sms, then I could unblock my MSFT account. Although I don't really need it, I only tried OneNote for 20 minutes, that's all.

ideas.title: Plug-In Piano
ideas.oneLiner: A tiny cross-platform app that detects your MIDI keyboard and gives you a good-sounding piano in one click, with optional practice plans for MIDI pieces you import.
ideas.problem: Someone who just wants to plug in a MIDI keyboard and play ends up fighting DAWs, VST hosts and drivers for days, while the polished practice apps sit behind expensive subscriptions.
ideas.targetUsers: Hobby pianists, choir members and music students with a USB or Bluetooth MIDI keyboard who are not producers.
ideas.monetization: Free basic piano; one-time Rs 1,499 / $19 for extra sound packs, practice plans and iPad sync. No subscription.
mvp: Auto-detect MIDI keyboard and play with no setup
One bundled quality piano sample set with a latency check
Import a MIDI file and show a falling-notes practice view
Simple practice plan: slow-down, loop a section, hands separate
Audio device picker with a one-click 'fix my sound' reset

competitors.name: GarageBand / Logic
competitors.gap: Apple-only and still a DAW; no Windows or Linux path.

competitors.name: Synthesia
competitors.gap: Practice-focused but needs separate sound setup for good tone.

competitors.name: Virtual MIDI Piano Keyboard (VMPK)
competitors.gap: Free and open source, but only a MIDI controller; it does not produce a good piano sound by itself.

competitors.name: Piano Marvel and similar subscription apps
competitors.gap: Good learning content, but the subscription pricing is exactly what users in these threads avoid.

sources.title: Comment on 'We don't need more apps, we need better open source'
sources.quote: I wanted to plug in my midi controller keyboard and just play a piano, so I can practice my choral music. Very basic. This turned into many hours over several days trying multiple DAWs, trying to get tehm to install, get them to run at all, get them to recognize my controller, get them to play a VST plugin...changing system settings, completely jacking up my sound, restoring it all again. It was a nightmare.

sources.title: Comment on 'We don't need more apps, we need better open source'
sources.quote: I have a similar experience where I’ve been learning the keyboard but didn’t like the available free options and the good paid apps had really expensive subscription plans so I had Claude build me something that runs natively on my iPad, with midi and microphone support and generates custom learning plans for midi pieces that I import.

ideas.title: DRM-Free Finder
ideas.oneLiner: A search site that shows where you can legally buy a given ebook, film or album as DRM-free files, with price and format.
ideas.problem: People say they would happily pay for DRM-free ebooks and films, but there is no single place to find which store sells which title without locks, so they fall back on Amazon or on piracy.
ideas.targetUsers: Readers, film fans and music listeners who want to own files, plus Indian users frustrated by regional pricing and platform lock-in.
ideas.monetization: Affiliate links to DRM-free stores (Kobo, Bandcamp, GOG, Smashwords, Humble and others); optional Rs 149/month supporter tier with wishlist alerts when a title goes DRM-free.
mvp: Search by title or ISBN that returns stores selling a DRM-free edition
Store directory with each store's DRM policy and formats
Wishlist alert when a title appears DRM-free or drops in price
Community flag when a listing is wrongly marked DRM-free
Filter by format (EPUB, FLAC, MP4) and price

competitors.name: GOG
competitors.gap: Excellent for games but has only a thin film and no ebook catalogue.

competitors.name: Kobo / Smashwords / Baen
competitors.gap: Mixed DRM per title, so buyers cannot tell in advance without checking each page.

competitors.name: AlternativeTo DRM-free list
competitors.gap: A static list of stores, not a per-title lookup.

sources.title: Comment on 'Many of Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday “deals” offered no savings'
sources.quote: Whats crazy is I'd happily pay a premium for a DRM free ebook, too.

sources.title: Comment on 'DNS resolvers are the wrong place to fight piracy'
sources.quote: For instance, if there were a site that offered movie downloads for $2-5 per movie, I'd happily pay for it. No DRM of course.

ideas.title: Script Graveyard
ideas.oneLiner: Scans a site for every third-party script and tag, shows who added it and whether it still fires, and generates a tighter Content-Security-Policy plus a one-click removal list.
ideas.problem: Marketing tags pile up and are forgotten, third-party URLs can break production, and a vendor compromise like the Optimizely incident reaches every site that pasted its tag. Teams cannot see what is loaded, who owns it, or whether anyone still uses it, and CSP rules for multi-country script domains are painful to maintain.
ideas.targetUsers: Agencies, freelancers and small-company devs who maintain marketing sites and shops they did not fully build.
ideas.monetization: Free single-site scan; $9/month per site for weekly rescans, new-script alerts and generated CSP; agency plan for 20 sites.
mvp: Crawl a URL and list all third-party scripts, domains and what they load next
Flag scripts that appear unused or unowned and let you record an owner
Generate a report-only CSP header with per-vendor domains, including country TLDs
Weekly rescan with an email when a new third-party script appears
Plain-language removal checklist for tag managers

competitors.name: Report URI
competitors.gap: Strong at monitoring script integrity, but aimed at teams already comfortable with CSP reporting.

competitors.name: Reflectiz
competitors.gap: Scanner-style data-flow mapping aimed at larger security and compliance teams.

competitors.name: Tag Inspector
competitors.gap: Enterprise privacy and marketing focus; heavy for a small site.

competitors.name: site-owner-infection-alert (earlier idea in this series)
competitors.gap: Alerts on known-malicious JavaScript; this idea is the inventory and cleanup side.

sources.title: Comment on 'Optimizely compromised, served malware on Zoom, GitLab'
sources.quote: I've had third party URLs block production apps in Chrome before because some marketing url was hosting malicious code. The most infuriating thing, when you do remove these tags, marketing forgets they exist and are like "Oh we don't use that anymore".

sources.title: Comment on 'Optimizely compromised, served malware on Zoom, GitLab'
sources.quote: And then there’s different countries for end clients with different TLDs for connect-src. Oh how I hate that one. I wish Facebook, Instagram, Google and others would figure out serving the public scripts from .com only.

sources.title: Comment on 'We know 15k websites are infected. how do we tell them?'
sources.quote: If we're really being serious about getting it fixed and not just waving a magic wand and laying blame, the scripts should not be distributed via a platform that tells web maintainers to blindly paste a script tag and leave their web servers wide open for the whitelisted 3rd party domain(s) to send whatever they want to visitors.

ideas.title: Registrar Scorecard
ideas.oneLiner: A comparison site that scores domain registrars on random ID checks, suspension history and support access, so you can pick one before you are locked out.
ideas.problem: Some registrars reportedly demand passports and selfies at random, with answers like 'we cannot specify the criteria', and a clientHold can take a whole site offline. People want to move but cannot tell which registrars will not do the same.
ideas.targetUsers: Developers, open-source projects, small businesses and agencies who own several domains.
ideas.monetization: Affiliate fees from registrars that score well; paid $4/month alert when your registrar's policy or reputation changes.
mvp: Standard questionnaire sent to registrars with published answers and dates
Score on ID-verification policy, hold and suspension process, and reachable support
Community reports of surprise verification or holds, with dates
Side-by-side comparison with renewal pricing
Move checklist linking to transfer steps

competitors.name: Generic registrar comparison blogs
competitors.gap: Compare price and features; they do not cover verification surprises or suspension handling.

competitors.name: domain-transfer-lockout-guard (earlier idea in this series)
competitors.gap: Checks that your own domains can be moved; it does not help you choose a trustworthy registrar.

sources.title: Comment on 'Codeberg seems to have vanished from DNS'
sources.quote: Apparently more and more registrars are "randomly" requiring clients to send copies of their passports and face selfies and other nonsense.

sources.title: Comment on 'Codeberg seems to have vanished from DNS'
sources.quote: Where are you moving to? Are there any registrars that have promised not to do this? Can we trust any of them? I'd rather not move once and then have to move again.

sources.title: Comment on 'Codeberg seems to have vanished from DNS'
sources.quote: I've been sending a questionnaire to a bunch of registrars with these questions. Namecheap failed spectacularly, others answered okay. It's a red flag if they don't list a sales or support email on their website, so that's another hint too.
